text: Inference is one word for two very different infrastructure problems. Batch inference scores a known pile of inputs on a schedule, and nobody's waiting synchronously on any single result — the metric that matters is throughput. Real-time inference answers one caller at a time inside a live request, and the metric that matters is p99 latency, the slowest one percent of responses. Build infrastructure for the wrong one and you either waste GPU spend or blow your latency budget.

A nightly job that re-scores ten million transactions for fraud risk doesn't need anything running around the clock — it needs to start, chew through the work as fast as possible, and stop. That's a Kubernetes Job, not a Deployment. Because a failed Job just retries from a checkpoint instead of breaking a live user flow, this is exactly the workload where Spot GPU instances make sense, and where you can push batch size far higher than any synchronous caller would tolerate.

A live chat app calling the model on every user turn is the opposite shape. A caller is blocked waiting right now, so the serving process has to already be warm and loaded into GPU memory behind a Service and Ingress before the request even arrives. Cold GPU startup can take minutes — loading weights, warming CUDA kernels — so real-time capacity is kept as a baseline of warm replicas instead of scaling from zero, and Spot interruptions are far riskier here than in batch.

Real-time inference still batches, just at the scale of milliseconds. A GPU can process eight or sixteen requests almost as fast as one, so serving frameworks use dynamic batching: hold incoming requests for a few milliseconds, group whatever arrived into a single GPU call, then return each caller its own slice of the result. It's the same throughput idea batch inference uses, compressed into a window short enough that nobody waiting synchronously notices.

That's the split to carry forward: Jobs and loose scheduling for batch, always-warm Deployments and tight latency budgets for real-time, and dynamic batching bridging the two inside the real-time path itself. Next lesson looks at the serving frameworks — Triton, TorchServe, KServe — that implement dynamic batching, model loading, and multi-model serving for you, instead of you hand-rolling every one of those pieces yourself.
